proposal.title: Supreme Court clears path for possible dismissal of Bannon contempt case
proposal.description_short: On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the appeals court ruling upholding Steve Bannon’s contempt conviction and remanded the case.

proposal.description_long: Steve Bannon was convicted in 2022 on two counts of contempt of Congress for refusing to provide documents or testimony to the House committee investigating the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. The D.C. Circuit upheld his conviction in May 2024, and the Supreme Court denied his request to remain out of prison while appealing in June 2024. Bannon served a four-month federal prison sentence later that year. On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the appellate judgment and remanded the matter. Reuters reported that DOJ told the Court dismissal was in the interests of justice and had already filed a dismissal motion in district court. The remand returned the case to the trial court for further proceedings; DOJ’s motion still required judicial action. The appellate judgment was vacated; the Supreme Court did not itself enter a dismissal. This account is limited to the procedural action and the government’s reported position.

proposal.title: Trump says he will always abide by courts during funding-freeze case
proposal.description_short: Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” as an appeals court rejected an emergency request in the funding-freeze dispute.
proposal.description_medium: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” while the administration challenged a lower-court order blocking a broad federal funding freeze. The First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate stay and left the district court to clarify the order’s scope. This records the February assurance; it does not support the original March claim that Trump said he could override court orders.
proposal.description_long: On February 11, 2025, President Donald Trump told ABC News he would “always abide by the courts” during a dispute over the administration’s effort to freeze federal funding. That day, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied the administration’s request for an immediate administrative stay of a lower-court order blocking the broad freeze. The appellate panel said it was uncertain what standards governed the requested stay and noted that the administration had not cited authority supporting it. The court left the district judge to clarify the scope of the earlier order and said it would consider a later request for a stay pending appeal. ABC reported that the administration argued the order improperly constrained executive spending authority, while state plaintiffs said a renewed freeze would harm recipients of federal funding. Trump’s brief assurance was made in this litigation context. It contradicts the held card’s claim that he declared he was not bound by court orders; the evidence supports recording the February statement and court response, not the alleged March declaration.

proposal.title: DOJ Challenges Maryland Court’s Automatic Immigration Injunctions
proposal.description_short: On June 25, 2025, DOJ announced a complaint challenging a Maryland court standing order that automatically enjoined some immigration removals.
proposal.description_medium: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland over a standing order requiring automatic injunctions when detained people filed habeas petitions. DOJ said the order blocked removal or challenges to their legal status and characterized the practice as judicial overreach. The release documents a legal challenge, not a refusal to obey court orders.
proposal.description_long: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland concerning the court’s standing order on immigration habeas petitions. According to DOJ’s release, the order instructed the court clerk to automatically enter an injunction against removing or challenging the legal status of a person detained in Maryland who filed a habeas petition. The department argued that the standing order conflicted with the requirements for preliminary injunctions and with Supreme Court precedent. Attorney General Pamela Bondi said that injunctions had impeded President Trump’s agenda and described the Maryland order as judicial overreach. The public statement documents DOJ’s formal challenge to a specific court procedure and its criticism of the judiciary. DOJ described the complaint as its latest action against what it called unlawful judicial overreach. It does not establish that Bondi refused to enforce multiple injunctions, as the original entry claimed.

The removal of commissioners was described as unprecedented by Reuters, which also reported that the former commissioners were considering legal action.
